deviations.aspect: Clarity slider response curve (strength per slider unit)
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Clarity is usable across its whole range: +10 to +25 is the normal working range recommended by Adobe and every tutorial, and the change from 0 to +25 is plainly visible. Adobe's own instruction ("increase the setting until you see halos near the edge details, then reduce slightly") only makes sense if small/medium values already do visible work. Negative clarity for portraits is likewise used at -10..-45.
deviations.our_behavior: The detail gain is `1 + gain·(1/alpha − 1)` with `gain = |c|/100`, `alpha = 1 − 0.6·gain` (ClarityMapping.swift:119-124, :54-55, :95). That is strongly convex, so the first half of the slider is nearly dead: local-contrast slope is 1.002 at +5, 1.006 at +10, 1.044 at +25, 1.214 at +50, 1.614 at +75, 2.500 at +100 (and 0.983 / 0.917 / 0.750 / 0.333 on the negative side). Clarity +10 changes local contrast by 0.6% — invisible; the entire perceptual range is squeezed into roughly +60..+100. The README's own measurement (README.md:311-314) needed clarity +80 to get a 1.65x texture gain.
deviations.proposed_fix: Make the effective lift roughly linear in the slider instead of the product of two ramps: e.g. `lift = kBoost · a` with kBoost ≈ 1.5 (and `lift = −kSmooth · a` with kSmooth ≈ 0.67) in `ClarityMapping.Parameters.lift`, or equivalently `gain = a^0.4`. One expression in ClarityMapping.swift:95/119-124; `lift = 0` at c = 0 stays exact, monotonicity bound `|lift| < 2.24` still holds, and no shader change is needed. Then re-anchor ±100 to "clearly too much" as in LR.

deviations.lightroom_behavior: Clarity is a midtone-targeted local contrast control. Adobe and all secondary sources describe it as adding contrast/depth to the midtones; highlights and deep shadows are protected, which is why heavy clarity does not blow highlights or crush blacks the way a global contrast push does, and why it "will not add grain to the highlight or shadow areas."
deviations.our_behavior: The lift is applied uniformly over the whole working range: the gamma grid spans −8..+3 EV with equal `lift` at every level (ClarityStage.swift:101-136, Clarity.metal:53-57), and the apply kernel scales by `amount` only, with no dependence on the pixel's tone (Clarity.metal:199-216). The only tonal shaping is the hard fade outside −8..+3 EV via weight clamping (ClarityMapping.swift:48-49, :183-186), which affects deep clipping levels, not midtone weighting. Bright textures near white and detail in deep shadows therefore get the same boost as midtones, and a positive clarity can push near-white detail over the clip point.
deviations.proposed_fix: Multiply the per-pixel amount by a tone weight in `clarityApplyKernel`: `a *= w(l0)` with e.g. `w(x) = exp(−((x − log2(0.18))/σ_t)²/2)`, σ_t ≈ 2.5-3 EV, clamped to a floor of ~0.2 so extremes are attenuated rather than switched off. Two lines in Clarity.metal:207-215 plus one uniform and a CPU mirror in ClarityMapping for tests. Free (no extra passes) and works identically for the masked case.

deviations.aspect: Clarity spatial frequency band (fine detail / noise amplification)
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Clarity is the mid/large-radius local-contrast control — "thicker edges", a larger radius than Texture. Texture is the mid-frequency control and was explicitly engineered to spare the finest high-frequency content so it does not amplify noise; Clarity sits coarser still. Neither is a sharpening/noise amplifier at pixel scale.
deviations.our_behavior: The fast local Laplacian lifts every Laplacian level with the same slope, including level 0 (Clarity.metal:167-180 accumulates `w_k · lap` at every level with no per-level weighting; ClarityStage.swift:125-135 loops `l in 0..<levels-1`). Level 0 is pixel-scale detail, i.e. sensor noise: at clarity +100 grain is multiplied by 2.5x exactly like real texture. The README already flags this (README.md:517-519) as a noise issue, but it is also a band mismatch — our clarity behaves like Clarity+Texture+a bit of sharpening in one slider.
deviations.proposed_fix: Add a per-level scale weight to the lift: pass `levelGain[l]` in `ClarityUniforms` and scale `u.lift` by it inside `grClarityRemap`/the accumulate pass, with e.g. gain 0 at level 0, ~0.4 at level 1 and 1.0 from level 2 up. Structurally this is one extra uniform in Clarity.metal + one array in ClarityStage.swift:101-136; it also makes room for a future Texture slider that uses the complementary weights.

deviations.aspect: Clarity edge behaviour / halos at high settings
deviations.lightroom_behavior: LR's Clarity produces visible halos at high settings — Adobe's own help text tells you to push it until halos appear and then back off. Much of the "clarity look" in B&W (broad tonal gradients hugging strong edges, the HiRaLoAm look) comes precisely from that large-radius, non-edge-aware component.
deviations.our_behavior: The Gaussian-windowed remap is deliberately halo-free: detail more than ~3 stops from the local mean passes through untouched (Clarity.metal:47-57, ClarityMapping.swift:147-150). Measured in README.md:311-314: 4 px from a 4-stop edge the flat region moves 0.0006 stops, versus 0.042 stops for an equivalent USM — 65x less. At high clarity our image gains micro-texture but never the broad edge gradients LR gives, so it reads as flatter/less dramatic on high-contrast B&W subjects.
deviations.proposed_fix: Blend a small, deliberately non-edge-aware component into the boost: `L_out = L + lift·(detail_LLF) + haloAmount·(L − blur_σ(L))` with σ ≈ 1-2% of the long edge and `haloAmount` a fraction of the clarity slider (0 at 0, ~0.15-0.25 at +100). One extra Gaussian (the existing pyramid can supply it: `L − upsample(G[3])`) plus one term in `clarityApplyKernel`. Keep it out of the negative side.

deviations.aspect: Negative clarity character (glow vs. detail flattening)
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Negative Clarity is a glow/bloom: light bleeds across edges, midtones lift slightly ("blurs out fine contrast in the midtones while adding white to the midtones"), and the result is the dreamy soft-focus/Orton look used for portraits at -10..-45. Edges stay defined but are surrounded by a halo of spilled light.
deviations.our_behavior: Negative clarity is the exact mirror of the positive case: the same Gaussian-windowed remap with a negative lift (ClarityMapping.swift:122, Clarity.metal:53-57), which *compresses* detail toward the local mean while explicitly leaving large edges alone and preserving the local mean. So there is no light spill across edges and no midtone lift — it reads as waxy/plastic detail removal, not glow. At -100 the detail slope is only 0.333 (and -25 gives 0.917, i.e. almost nothing; see the response-curve entry).
deviations.proposed_fix: Give the negative side its own operator instead of reusing the mirrored remap: for c < 0 compute `L_glow = max(L, blur_σ(L))` (or a screen blend of L with a Gaussian-blurred L, σ ≈ 1% of long edge) and set `L_out = mix(L, L_glow, k·|c|/100)` combined with a mild detail attenuation. That is one extra blur (the Gaussian pyramid is already built) and a separate branch in `clarityApplyKernel`; it also gives the midtone lift LR has. Keeps the positive path untouched.

deviations.aspect: Local clarity with opposite sign to the global slider (negative-clarity skin brush under positive global clarity)
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Each mask's Clarity is independent of the global Clarity and of every other mask. Global Clarity +30 with a -60 Clarity brush on skin is a canonical portrait recipe and produces genuinely softened skin while the rest of the frame keeps its local contrast.
deviations.our_behavior: Only one local-Laplacian variant is rendered per frame, of the dominant sign, and pixels whose accumulated clarity has the opposite sign are clamped to amount 0 (MaskRasterizer.swift:246-250, Mask.metal:145-154, Pipeline.swift:100-120). With global +30 and a -60 mask, the range is [-30, +30], the tie goes to the positive variant, and the masked pixels get amount 0: the skin is merely *excluded* from the global clarity, never softened. The behaviour is documented as deliberate (README.md:340-347) but it silently drops a slider the user moved.
deviations.proposed_fix: Run the stage twice when `clarityRange` straddles zero: compute `L_boost` and `L_smooth`, build two amount maps (positive and negative side) and apply `L_out = L + a_pos·(L_boost − L) + a_neg·(L_smooth − L)`. `ClarityStage.encode` already takes an amount texture, so this is a second `encode` into a scratch texture plus a 4-input apply kernel. Cheaper alternative if the cost is unacceptable: only run the second pass when the minority-sign magnitude exceeds a threshold (e.g. 10), and warn otherwise.

deviations.aspect: Local clarity masks change the clarity rendering outside the mask
deviations.lightroom_behavior: A local Clarity adjustment affects only the masked pixels. Adding a +20 Clarity mask never changes how the global Clarity renders elsewhere in the frame.
deviations.our_behavior: `L_llf` is computed once at the frame's maximum |clarity| and blended linearly: `amount(x) = clamp(sign·c(x), 0, |c_max|)/|c_max|` (Mask.metal:145-154, MaskRasterizer.swift:225-233). Because the strength mapping is strongly nonlinear, a linear blend of a strong variant is not the weak variant. Concretely: global 25 with a +20 mask gives c_max = 45 and amount 25/45 outside the mask, which yields an effective detail slope of 1.093 — the same as clarity ≈35, not 25. Worse with disjoint masks: `clarityRange` sums *all* positive deltas regardless of overlap (MaskRasterizer.swift:225-233), so two disjoint +50 masks give c_max = 100 and each mask region renders at slope 1.75 instead of 1.214. The README measures only a 0.1% luminance shift (README.md:348-353) because its test image has low detail amplitude; in slider terms the error is 40%+.
deviations.proposed_fix: Make the amount map compensate for the nonlinearity instead of being linear in the slider: `amount(x) = lift(c(x)) / lift(c_max)` where `lift` is `ClarityMapping.Parameters.lift`. In the linearised regime this reproduces each pixel's own strength exactly. It is ~5 lines in `maskClarityAmountKernel` (Mask.metal:145-154) plus passing `lift(c_max)` as a uniform, and it subsumes the disjoint-mask over-estimate. (If the response curve is linearised per the first entry, this reduces to the current code — do that one first.)

deviations.lightroom_behavior: Flow is the rate of application and is cumulative *across* strokes: "keep brushing and more is applied"; with a low Flow "it will take longer and require more passes", and the adjustment "does eventually reach its full strength" (bounded by Density). This is the core dodge-and-burn mechanic — repeated light passes let you sculpt coverage.
deviations.our_behavior: Each stroke is rasterised into its own buffer, clamped at density, then merged with `max(mask, stroke)` (MaskRasterizer.swift:132-166, Mask.metal:83-88). Over-compositing happens only *within* one stroke. Repainting the same area with the same brush therefore adds nothing: `max(x, x) = x`. Ten passes at flow 20 give exactly what one pass gives. Additionally the within-stroke build-up makes a *single* pass far stronger than LR's: with spacing 0.15·diameter, ~7 stamps overlap on the centreline, so one straight stroke at flow 20 / feather 50 already reaches 0.67 coverage (flow 10 → 0.41, flow 50 → 0.97). Flow is effectively a compressed one-shot opacity control rather than a rate.
deviations.proposed_fix: Swap the two composite rules (the standard non-incremental paint model): within a stroke use `acc = max(acc, alpha)` (Mask.metal:83, MaskRasterizer.swift:151) so one pass deposits ~flow; across strokes over-composite toward the density cap, `m = min(m + acc·(1 − m), max(m, density))` for a paint stroke (Mask.metal:88, MaskRasterizer.swift:156-165). Erase keeps `m·(1 − acc)`. Same number of dispatches, no format changes; the existing GPU-vs-CPU parity test covers both sides.

deviations.aspect: Brush Density as an absolute ceiling
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Density caps the maximum opacity that brushing can ever reach in an area, "no matter how many times you stroke it" — including across separate strokes and across the whole build-up sequence.
deviations.our_behavior: Density is clamped per *stroke* buffer only (MaskRasterizer.swift:156-165, Mask.metal:85, Mask.swift:174-176 doc). With `max` merging that happens to bound the mask today, but it is the wrong invariant: as soon as cross-stroke build-up is added (previous entry) the cap must be applied to the merged mask, not the stroke. Also, LR's cap is a property of the brush at paint time — painting at density 40 over an area already at 0.8 must leave it at 0.8, not pull it down.
deviations.proposed_fix: Apply the ceiling at merge time as `m = min(m + acc·(1 − m), max(m, density))`, which both caps build-up at `density` and never lowers existing coverage. Land it together with the flow fix; it is the same two lines.

deviations.aspect: Overlapping mask composition and range clamping
deviations.lightroom_behavior: Each mask is an independent local adjustment; multiple masks over the same pixels compound. Stacking a second brush/mask over the same area to push past a single mask's ±4 EV limit is a standard technique, and there is no global ceiling on the combined result. Each mask's tone adjustment is applied as its own transform, not by adding slider numbers.
deviations.our_behavior: All masks accumulate into two shared parameter textures and the *sum* is clamped once at ±4 EV / ±100 (MaskStage.swift:113-155, Mask.metal:107-135, MaskRasterizer.swift:197-218, Mask.swift:81-82). Two overlapping +3 EV masks give +4 EV, not +6 EV; two +80 shadows masks give +100, not "+80 applied twice". The per-pixel delta vector is then evaluated once as a single curve delta (README.md:153-186), so local sliders are additive in slider units rather than composed — which is a different curve from LR's sequential application for anything but pure exposure.
deviations.proposed_fix: Two independent steps. (a) Cheap: raise or drop the accumulation ceiling — clamp exposure to something like ±8 EV (or not at all, letting the tone stage's own range limit it) rather than to the single-mask ±4 EV, so overlaps compound as in LR. That is the constants in Mask.swift:81-82 plus `MaskClampUniforms`. (b) Structural: to match LR's composition, evaluate masks sequentially (each mask's curve applied to the previous result) instead of summing deltas — that means either N tone passes or an ordered per-pixel loop, and is only worth it if (a) proves insufficient.

deviations.lightroom_behavior: The brush has an Auto Mask option that "confines brush strokes to areas of similar color", with improved noise handling from PV4. It is what makes edge-following dodge/burn (skyline, horizon, subject outline) practical without a separate selection.
deviations.our_behavior: Not implemented. Coverage depends only on stroke geometry (MaskRasterizer.swift:127-168, Mask.metal:62-90); there is no image-dependent term anywhere in the mask path, and README.md:510-516 lists "no guided-filter edge snapping" as a known limitation. Painting a brightening mask along a horizon spills across it and has to be cleaned up with an erase stroke.
deviations.proposed_fix: Post-process each mask's coverage with a guided filter (He et al.) using the tone-stage luminance as guide, gated by a per-stroke `autoMask` flag; or the cheaper LR-1.x-style variant: sample the guide luminance at the stroke's first point and multiply each stamp's alpha by a similarity kernel on |L(x) − L_ref|. The second version is a ~30-line shader change and needs the tone output bound into `maskStrokeKernel`, but the mask cache must then also key on the tone parameters.

deviations.lightroom_behavior: Clarity measurably changes saturation as well as luminance — it is not a pure luminance operation, which is one of the standard reasons cited for preferring Texture when you want detail without a colour shift.
deviations.our_behavior: Clarity is applied as a pure multiplicative luminance ratio, `rgb' = rgb · 2^(L_out − L)` (Clarity.metal:199-216), which leaves channel ratios and therefore HSV saturation exactly unchanged by construction (README.md:205-216). In a B&W-only pipeline the direct visual effect is nil, but clarity runs *before* the saturation-weighted B&W mixer (Pipeline.swift:97-123), so in LR a clarity push slightly increases the mixer's authority in boosted regions and here it does not.
deviations.proposed_fix: Probably leave as is — the hue/ratio-preserving design is a stated goal and the B&W-visible difference is second order. If matching is wanted, scale saturation by a small function of the applied `dL` in `clarityApplyKernel` (e.g. push rgb away from its luminance by `1 + kSat·dL`), which needs a saturation clamp to avoid gamut blow-ups.

deviations.lightroom_behavior: The brush offers two switchable presets, A and B, plus a separate Erase brush, each holding its own Size/Feather/Flow/Density — so you can flip between e.g. a big soft low-flow burn brush and a small hard detail brush without re-setting four sliders.
deviations.our_behavior: One live `BrushParams` in the UI store (GrayroomUI/EditStateStore.swift:53, GrayroomApp/Sidebar.swift:337-354). `Stroke` already carries its own `BrushParams` (Mask.swift:133-160), so the model supports it; only the UI state and the switch are missing. Erase is a mode flag rather than a brush with its own settings.
deviations.proposed_fix: Store three `BrushParams` in `EditStateStore` (A, B, Erase) plus a selected-slot enum, bind the sliders to the active slot, and add a keyboard toggle (LR uses `/`). No core change.

notes:
Scope: read-only audit of Sources/GrayroomCore/Shaders/Clarity.metal, Stages/ClarityMapping.swift, Stages/ClarityStage.swift, Masks/{Mask,MaskRasterizer,MaskStage}.swift, Shaders/Mask.metal, Engine/Pipeline.swift, plus the clarity/mask sections of Sources/GrayroomCore/README.md. Nothing was modified and no build/test was run.

Two numbers I computed rather than read (scripts in the scratchpad, both derived directly from the code's own formulas):
1. Clarity detail-slope vs slider, from ClarityMapping.Parameters.lift: +5 -> 1.002, +10 -> 1.006, +25 -> 1.044, +50 -> 1.214, +75 -> 1.614, +100 -> 2.500; negative side 0.995 / 0.983 / 0.917 / 0.750 / 0.333. This is the single biggest calibration gap and it also amplifies the mask-amount error (entry "Local clarity masks change the clarity rendering outside the mask") - fixing the response curve first makes that one nearly disappear.
2. Single-stroke centreline coverage from the stamp model (spacing 0.15*diameter -> ~7 overlapping stamps): feather 50 gives 0.41 / 0.67 / 0.83 / 0.97 / 1.00 at flow 10 / 20 / 30 / 50 / 100. Combined with max-merge across strokes this is why flow reads as a one-shot opacity instead of a rate.

Confidence caveats worth flagging to the maintainer:
- Adobe has never published Clarity's algorithm; the "midtone-weighted", "larger radius than Texture" and "affects saturation" claims come from Adobe help/blog wording plus consistent secondary reporting, not from a measurement. I marked the frequency-band and midtone entries "documented" because Adobe's own Texture write-up and help text support them, but the exact weighting curve is guesswork - any implementation should be tuned by eye against LR renders of the same file, not against a formula.
- I could not find a published measurement of LR's absolute clarity strength at +-100, so I did not claim ours is "stronger" or "weaker" overall. The defensible statement is about the *shape* of the response (ours is dead below ~+40) and about the band (ours boosts pixel-scale detail, LR's does not), not the endpoint magnitude. Marked that entry "inferred".
- LR's exact within-stroke build-up rule is not documented; sources agree only that (a) flow builds across passes and (b) density is a hard ceiling. The proposed max-within-stroke / over-composite-across-strokes model is the standard non-incremental paint model (GIMP calls it the "Incremental" toggle) and matches both documented facts, but a maintainer with LR available should verify a single straight stroke at flow 20 measures ~20% before committing to it.

Things I deliberately did NOT report as deviations: the fused level-0 remap, the 16-level gamma grid, texture ping-ponging, r16Float coverage, the one-entry mask cache, and the 0.1% luminance drift the README already measures for the single-variant blend on its test image - all implementation detail or below any plausible visibility threshold. I also skipped preview-vs-export resolution dependence of the pyramid depth, since LR has the same class of behaviour.
